source_title: Currency movements, taxation: Risks to know before investing abroad - Business Standard
source_excerpt: Investing abroad has become mainstream for Indian retail investors. International mutual funds, exchange-traded funds, overseas brokerage platforms and liberalised remittance rules have made foreign markets easier to access than ever before. People want to invest in businesses and sectors that have limited representation in Indian markets. Technology giants, semiconductor manufacturers, healthcare innovators and global consumer brands draw strong interest from Indian households looking to diversify wealth beyond domestic equities. That said, foreign investments are shaped by currency movements, taxation rules, geopolitical developments and economic cycles that behave differently from India’s markets. Financial advisers say that international diversification can strengthen long-term portfolios, but investors must understand what they are taking exposure to before allocating capital abroad. Currency risk can impact returnsCurrency fluctuation is one of the biggest risks in overseas investing. When Indian investors buy assets denominated in dollars, euros or other foreign currencies, final returns depend heavily on exchange-rate movements. Even a strong-performing investment can generate weaker returns if the rupee appreciates sharply against the foreign currency during the holding period. The reverse is equally true. Investors in US equities benefited significantly over the past decade because the dollar strengthened against the rupee for extended periods. Currency depreciation amplified gains when those investments were converted back into Indian currency. This relationship becomes especially important during periods of global uncertainty. Central bank decisions, oil-price volatility, trade tensions and geopolitical conflicts can all influence currency markets within days. For Indian investors, overseas exposure effectively introduces a second layer of volatility. The underlying investment may remain stable while currency swings alter actual portfolio returns substantially. Taxation can reduce net gainsTax treatment is another area where many retail investors lack clarity. International investments often involve withholding taxes on dividends in the foreign jurisdiction. Investors may then face additional taxation in India depending on the nature of the investment and prevailing tax rules. Double taxation avoidance agreements can provide relief in certain cases, though compliance requirements may remain complicated for individual investors. Capital gains taxation also differs depending on whether exposure is taken through direct equities, international mutual funds or exchange-traded products. Tax rules surrounding overseas investing have evolved significantly in recent years, particularly after changes in debt-fund taxation and global mutual fund classifications. Investors focusing purely on headline returns often ignore the impact of taxation on final wealth creation. Global markets have different cyclesOne of the main reasons investors allocate money internationally is to reduce concentration risk. However, foreign markets operate under different economic and policy environments. The US, Europe, China and emerging economies often move through separate growth and interest-rate cycles. A rally in Indian equities may coincide with weakness in global technology stocks. Commodity-driven economies may outperform during inflationary periods while developed markets struggle with slowing growth. This can create discomfort for investors accustomed to domestic market behaviour. For instance, US technology stocks witnessed sharp valuation corrections when interest rates rose aggressively after the pandemic-era liquidity boom. Many Indian investors who entered global technology themes near peak valuations experienced steep drawdowns despite remaining optimistic about long-term growth prospects. Global diversification therefore reduces dependence on a single economy, but it does not eliminate volatility. Geopolitical risks carry greater influenceInternational portfolios are far more exposed to geopolitical events than many retail investors realise. Wars, sanctions, trade restrictions, diplomatic tensions and supply-chain disruptions can quickly alter global investor sentiment. Energy prices, shipping costs and commodity availability often react immediately to political developments across regions. Semiconductor companies remain sensitive to tensions involving Taiwan and China. European industries continue to respond sharply to energy disruptions and regional security concerns. Global technology companies face regulatory pressure from multiple governments simultaneously. Indian investors entering overseas markets must therefore follow a broader set of global developments compared to domestic investing. Market corrections abroad are often triggered by events that may appear geographically distant but still affect portfolio returns significantly. Information does not mean understandingAccess to global investing platforms and financial content has increased dramatically over the past few years. Yet, information availability does not automatically improve investment judgement. Social media trends, for instance, have encouraged aggressive participation in themes such as artificial intelligence, electric vehicles and clean energy without adequate attention to valuation, profitability or business quality. Retail investors often develop familiarity with global brands as consumers and mistake that familiarity for investment conviction. Foreign markets also operate under different accounting standards, governance frameworks and regulatory structures. Investors with limited understanding of local conditions may struggle to evaluate risks effectively. Financial advisers say overseas investing requires the same discipline and due diligence as domestic investing. Global visibility should not replace fundamental analysis. Allocation matters more than excitementMost wealth managers support moderate international exposure within diversified portfolios. Overseas investments can provide access to sectors unavailable in India and reduce overdependence on domestic economic cycles. However, excessive allocation towards global assets can create concentration risk of a different kind. Currency weakness, prolonged downturns in foreign markets or regulatory shifts can weigh heavily on portfolios with aggressive overseas exposure. The right allocation depends on age, financial goals, investment horizon and overall asset mix. Younger investors with longer horizons may absorb international volatility more comfortably. Investors nearing major financial goals may require greater emphasis on stability and liquidity instead of aggressive global positioning. FAQsWhat is the biggest mistake investors make while investing abroad?Many investors chase global trends without understanding currency risk, taxation or valuation levels. Successful international investing requires patience, diversification and a long-term approach. How much tax will I pay if investing in global stocks?Indian investors pay tax on global stocks through capital gains tax and taxation on dividends, with rates depending on holding period and income slab. Foreign countries may also deduct withholding tax on dividends, though tax credits can often be claimed in India under double taxation treaties. What laws regulate foreign investing in India?Foreign investing by Indian residents is primarily regulated under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme of the Reserve Bank of India and the Foreign Exchange Management Act. Taxation and disclosure requirements are governed by the Income Tax Act, while overseas investment routes through mutual funds and brokers are additionally overseen by the Securities and Exchange Board of India.
